DETAILED ACTION
This non-final office action is in response to claims 1-21 filed on 02/01/2021 for examination. Claims 1-21 are being examined and pending.
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Information Disclosure Statement
No information disclosure statement (IDS) is submitted.
Drawings
The drawings filed on 02/01/2021 have been accepted.
Claim Objections
Claim 1, 4, 8, 11, 12, 14, and 19 are objected because of following minor informality:
In line 8 of claim 1, examiner suggests to replace “ the unique portions “ with - - the unique portion - -. Same applies to claim 11 and 12.
In line 1 of claim 4, examiner suggests to replace “at least” with - - at least one of - -.
In line 4 of claim 8 and 19, examiner suggests to replace “ the repository hash” with - - a repository hash - - and replace “a repository hash” with - - the repository hash - -.
In line 1 of claim 14, examiner suggests to replace “the system of claim 1” with - - the system of claim 12 - -.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claim 1-21 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA  the applicant regards as the invention
Regarding claim 1, 11 and 12, they recite “ the unique portion” in line 7. There is lack of antecedent for “the unique portion” because there is no “unique portion” recited prior. Therefore it’s not clear which unique portion that “the unique portion” refer to.
Regarding claim 9 and 20, they both recite “ the at least a resource artifact” multiple times. There is lack of antecedent for “the at least a resource artifact” because there is no “at least a resource artifact” recited prior. Therefore it’s not clear which resource artifact that “the at least a resource artifact” refer to.
Regarding claim 10 and 21, they both recite “the artifact source” in line 2. There is lack of antecedent for “the artifact source” because there are two “an artifact source” recited prior. Therefore it’s not clear which artifact source that “the artifact source” refer to.
Dependent claims 2-8 and 13-19 are rejected with same deficiencies.
Regarding claim 9 and 20, the scope of “when executed, generates the at least a resource artifact” is not clear. The claim 9 and 20 recites determining an artifact source of the at least a resource artifact, wherein an artifact source is at least a software package version, wherein the at least a software package version, therefore it’s not clear how to execute a software package version to generate a resource artifact.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 101 (Abstract Idea)
35 U.S.C. 101 reads as follows: Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
Amended claims 1-21 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to an abstract idea without significantly more analyzed according to 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (“2019 PEG”). The claim recites a method for storing data using bidirectional linked blockchain.
Regarding independent claims 1, 11 and 12,
Step 1: The claims 1, 11 and 12 do fall into one of the four statutory categories of method and system. Nevertheless the claims 1, 11 and 12 still are considered as abstract idea for the following prongs and reasons.
Step 2A: Prong 1: The limitation of claims 1, 11 and 12 recite: inspecting a plurality of computing resources to detect code……; filtering the detected code to remove a portion of the code….; performing static analysis on the unique portion of the code…..; and comparing each identified mismatch……, as drafted, is a process that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance of the limitation in the mind and / or with pen and paper, there is nothing in the claim element precludes the step from practically being performed in the mind and with pen and paper. For example, inspecting device to detect code, filtering the detected code, perform static analysis and comparing …with mismatch…... Thus, the claims 1, 11 and 12 recite a mental process.
Prong 2: This judicial exception is not integrated into a practical application. In particular, the claims do not recite any additional element to perform beyond inspecting, filtering and comparing. The combination of those steps are recited at a high-level of generality such that it amounts no more than mere instructions to apply the exception using generic computer components. Accordingly, this additional element does not integrate the abstract idea into a practical application because it does not impose any meaningful limits on practicing the abstract idea. Therefore the claims 1, 11 and 12 are directed to an abstract idea.
Step 2B: The claim does not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. As discussed above with respect to integration of the abstract idea into a practical application, recited claims amount to no more than mere instructions to apply the exception using a generic computer terms. Mere instructions to apply an exception using a generic computer components cannot provide an inventive concept. The claim 1, 11 and 12 are not patent eligible. Therefore all claims 1, 11 and 12 are rejected under 35 USC 101 (abstract idea)
The dependent claims 2-10 and 13-21 have also been fully analyzed. Each of these dependent claims are mere recites additional abstract idea or an insignificant, extra-solution activity. Therefore, the dependent claims also fail to integrate the abstract idea into a practical application. Moreover, the claims have also been analyzed regarding whether they recite significantly more than the abstract idea. The dependent claims fail to add significantly more than the abstract idea. Therefore all claims 2-10 and 13-21 are rejected under 35 USC 101 (abstract idea)
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(a)(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claim 1-3 and 11-14  are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by  Gupta et al. US20150356451, hereinafter Gupta).
Regarding claim 1, 11, and 12, Gupta teaches a method for detection of cyber threats embedded in cloud applications (Gupta: a system/method to quickly and efficiently identify software-application behaviors that are not benign; Fig. 3, cloud 118, cloud unit 302; Para. 0013 and 0028), comprising inspecting a plurality of computing resources to detect code of at least one cloud application executed in a cloud environment (Gupta: upon receiving the application binary file from an app store (on the cloud), perform binary analysis on method calls, functions to identify features/characteristics/artifact of the application; Para. 0095, 0103); filtering the detected code to remove a portion of the code that is non-unique for the at least one cloud application (Gupta: remove generic features from extracted features to produce a set of application-specific features; Fig. 5, S502 and S506, Para. 0096-0097 and 0124); performing static analysis on the unique portion of the code to identify a mismatch between the unique portions of the code and its verified version stored in a code repository (Gupta: the lightweight binary analysis includes a static analysis of the binary file, derive features specific to the application based on the analysis, generate a behavior vector for the application based on the observed behaviors, apply the generated behavior vector to the classifier model ; Fig. 4, S404, S412, Fig. 9, S906 and S908; Para. 0103, 0124 and 0117); and comparing each identified mismatch with at least a vulnerability tool, wherein a mismatch is a potential cyber threat embedded in the code (Gupta: the classifier unit 208 receives the behavior vector and compares with the classifier model to determine whether the application (related to online credit card transaction) is not benign; Fig. 4: S416; Para. 0075 and 0119).
Regarding claim 2 and 13, Gupta teaches the method of claim 1. In addition, Gupta further teaches reporting each identified potential cyber threat (Gupta: Para. 0076-0077).
Regarding claim 3 and 14, Gupta teaches the method of claim 1. In addition, Gupta further teaches comparing the non-unique code portions to a vulnerability database to determine if the non-unique portion of the code contains known vulnerabilities (Gupta: Para. 0189).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention(s) absent any evidence to the contrary.  Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of each claim that was not commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the later invention in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) for any potential 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) prior art against the later invention.
Claim 4 and 15 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gupta in view of Vaishnavi (US20200272670, hereinafter Vai).
Regarding claim 4 and 15, Gupta teaches the method of claim 3.
Yet, Gupta does not teach wherein the non-unique portion includes at least: an operating system (OS) package data feature, and a third-party code library data feature
However, in the same field of endeavor, Vai teaches wherein the non-unique portion includes at least: an operating system (OS) package data feature, and a third-party code library data feature (Vai: Para. 0076 and 0111).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filling date of the claimed invention to modify the method disclosed by Gupta to include wherein the non-unique portion includes at least: an operating system (OS) package data feature, and a third-party code library data feature as disclosed by Vai. One of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to make this modification in order to identify shared/common libraries across cloud services as suggested by Vai (Vai: Para. 0076).
Claim 5-6 and 16-17 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gupta in view of Vai, and further in view of Kavi (US20180176262).
Regarding claim 5 and 16, combination of Gupta and Vai teaches the method of claim 4.
Yet, the combination does not teach wherein identifying the mismatch between the unique portion of the code and its verified version stored in the code repository further comprises: comparing hash values of the unique portion of the code to hash values of its verified version
However, in the same field of endeavor, Kavi teaches wherein identifying the mismatch between the unique portion of the code and its verified version stored in the code repository further comprises: comparing hash values of the unique portion of the code to hash values of its verified version (Kavi: Para. 0040).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filling date of the claimed invention to modify the method disclosed by the combination to include wherein identifying the mismatch between the unique portion of the code and its verified version stored in the code repository further comprises: comparing hash values of the unique portion of the code to hash values of its verified version as disclosed by Kavi. One of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to make this modification in order to prevent corruption of source code as suggested by Kavi (Kavi: Para. 0040).
Regarding claim 6 and 17, combination of Gupta, Vai and Kavi teaches the method of claim 5. In addition, Gupta teaches wherein the code includes any one of: binary code, executable code, and high-level programming language code (Gupta: binary, Para. 0095).
Claim 7-9 and 18-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gupta in view of Baierlein et al. (US20200371782, hereinafter Bai).
Regarding claim 7 and 18, Gupta teaches the method of claim 1.
Yet, Gupta does not teach wherein the code includes artifacts, and wherein the method further comprises scanning the artifacts for cyber threats.
However, in the same field of endeavor, Bai teaches wherein the code includes artifacts, and wherein the method further comprises scanning the artifacts for cyber threats (Bai: Para. 0060, 0079-0081).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filling date of the claimed invention to modify the method disclosed by Gupta to include wherein the code includes artifacts, and wherein the method further comprises scanning the artifacts for cyber threats as disclosed by Bai. One of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to make this modification in order to monitor artifacts to detect malicious code as suggested by Bai (Bai: Para. 0072 and 0079).
Regarding claim 8 and 19, Gupta teaches the method of claim 1.
Yet, Gupta does not teach creating a resource artifact hash, wherein the resource artifact hash is a low-file- size representation of a resource artifact included in the code; and comparing the resource artifact hash with the repository hash, wherein a repository hash is a low-file-size representation of an artifact included in a repository.
However, in the same field of endeavor, Bai teaches creating a resource artifact hash, wherein the resource artifact hash is a low-file- size representation of a resource artifact included in the code (Bai: Para. 0061, 0084); and comparing the resource artifact hash with the repository hash, wherein a repository hash is a low-file-size representation of an artifact included in a repository (Bai: Para. 0092).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filling date of the claimed invention to modify the method disclosed by Gupta to include creating a resource artifact hash, wherein the resource artifact hash is a low-file- size representation of a resource artifact included in the code; and comparing the resource artifact hash with the repository hash, wherein a repository hash is a low-file-size representation of an artifact included in a repository  as disclosed by Bai. One of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to make this modification in order to monitor artifacts to detect malicious code as suggested by Bai (Bai: Para. 0072 and 0079).
Regarding claim 9 and 20, Gupta teaches the method of claim 1.
Yet, Gupta does not teach determining an artifact status of the resource artifact, wherein an artifact status of the at least a resource artifact is a descriptor indicating the status of the at least a resource artifact; and determining an artifact source of the at least a resource artifact, wherein an artifact source is at least a software package version, wherein the at least a software package version, when executed, generates the at least a resource artifact.
However, in the same field of endeavor, Bai teaches determining an artifact status of the resource artifact, wherein an artifact status of the at least a resource artifact is a descriptor indicating the status of the at least a resource artifact (Bai: Para. 0026); and determining an artifact source of the at least a resource artifact, wherein an artifact source is at least a software package version, wherein the at least a software package version, when executed, generates the at least a resource artifact (Bai: Para. 0069, 0076 and 0098).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filling date of the claimed invention to modify the method disclosed by Gupta to include determining an artifact status of the resource artifact, wherein an artifact status of the at least a resource artifact is a descriptor indicating the status of the at least a resource artifact; and determining an artifact source of the at least a resource artifact, wherein an artifact source is at least a software package version, wherein the at least a software package version, when executed, generates the at least a resource artifact as disclosed by Bai. One of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to make this modification in order to monitor artifacts to detect malicious code as suggested by Bai (Bai: Para. 0072 and 0079).
Claim 10 and 21 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gupta in view of Bai, and further in view of  Freitag et al. (US10691810, hereinafter Frei).
Regarding claim 10 and 21, combination of Gupta and Bai teaches the method of claim 9. In addition, Bai further teaches determining if the resource artifact contains vulnerabilities (Bai: monitoring artifacts to detect malicious code; Para. 0072, 0079, 0080, 0102)
Yet, the combination does not teach determining if the resource artifact contains vulnerabilities based on the artifact status and the artifact source.
However, in the same field of endeavor, Frei teaches determining if the resource artifact contains vulnerabilities based on the artifact status and the artifact source (Frei: Col. 7, line 38-63).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filling date of the claimed invention to modify the method disclosed by the combination to include determining if the resource artifact contains vulnerabilities based on the artifact status and the artifact source  as disclosed by Frei. One of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to make this modification in order to detect vulnerabilities associated with a software application build as suggested by Frei (Frei: Col. 4, line 15-16).
Conclusion
The prior art made of record and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure:
Haghighat et al. (US20210263779): system load common code libraries, Para. 0688; calculate hash of container value, Para. 0744; comparing hash value with stored hash in the table, Para. 0749.
